newsitem.title: CANADA: FOCUS-Canadian financial markets weaken sharply.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Canadian financial markets weaken sharply.

text.p: Canadian financial markets weakened sharply on Thursday, with traders citing several causes for what they called a "made-in-Canada meltdown."
Canadian bonds, stocks and the dollar all ended the session sharply lower in a broad-based selloff.

"I don't think you can lay your finger on any single factor. It's a number of events that are happening in a reasonably thin market," said Mark Chandler, a senior economist with Goldman Sachs Canada. "I think you can argue the genesis of it was the weakness in the currency."

The Canadian dollar opened sharply weaker this morning, softening past the key C$1.3600 (US$0.7353) level. The dollar's weakness prompted the Bank of Canada to intervene in the currency markets several times, buying Canadian dollars for U.S. dollars.

Analysts tied the markets' drop to waning expectations about another Bank of Canada interest rate cut, investors withdrawing bets that Canadian bonds would outperform U.S. issues and attempts by traders to lock in profits.

Dealers said the weaker currency made a near-term rate cut by the central bank highly unlikely. Many traders had expected a cut in order to loosen monetary conditions and spur economic growth in Canada.
Analysts said the weaker dollar achieved the same effect by making Canadian exports more competitive.
Weakness in the currency and waning rate cut hopes contributed to -- but were also partly caused by -- weakness in Canadian bonds, analysts said.

Canadian bond prices plunged by mid-morning, posting some of their largest one-day losses in more than two years. Canada's benchmark 30-year bond recovered slightly by midafternoon, but was still down C$3.10 to C$110.85 with a yield of 7.086 percent.
Analysts said the selling came from domestic and foreign investors, who made profits this year betting that Canadian bonds would strengthen more than those in the United States.
Dealers said too many investors tried to sell Canadian bonds on Thursday to try to lock in profits before year end, causing prices to erode.

"In Canada, when everyone runs for the door at the same time, it creates a little bit of a bottleneck," said Michael Gregory, an economist and strategist with Lehman Brothers. "It has not been a lot of players. It's just a lot of big money leaving at the same time."

The selloff in the bond market and waning rate cut expectations in turn hurt the Canadian stock market, analysts said. The benchmark Toronto Stock Exchange 300 index was down more than one percent on the day, despite gains on Wall Street, which Toronto usually tracks.
Stocks were led lower by financial services and bank stocks, which are the most heavily weighed subgroup of the 300 index.

Dealers were mixed on the near-term outlook for Canadian financial markets. Although Canada's positive fundamentals, such as low inflation, remain in place, investors will be keenly studying key November employment data due on Friday.

"The thing to watch out for obviously is the (Canada and U.S.) payroll reports," said Goldman's Chandler. "If we get positive surprises in terms of growth there, you could get more follow-through selling."
